title: Honey-Glazed French Crullers
summary: Ridged rings of choux paste fried until crisp and airy, then dipped in a thin honey glaze.
equipment: stand mixer with paddle (or hand mixer)
piping bag with a 1.5 cm open star nozzle
10 squares of baking paper (10 cm), lightly oiled
large heavy pan or casserole, at least 24 cm wide
wire rack over a tray lined with kitchen paper

ingredients.item: fine sea salt or table salt
large eggs, plus 1 egg white, beaten together
neutral frying oil (sunflower, rapeseed or vegetable)

steps.title: Cook the paste
steps.text: Bring the water, milk, butter, sugar and salt to the boil in the saucepan. Take it off the heat, add the flour all at once and beat until smooth. Put it back over medium heat and keep stirring for about 2 min, until a thin film forms on the base of the pan.

steps.title: Cool it
steps.text: Tip the paste into the mixer bowl and beat on low for 2-3 min until it feels just warm, below 50 °C.

steps.title: Beat in the eggs
steps.text: Add the beaten eggs and vanilla in four goes, beating well after each, until the paste is glossy and drops from the paddle in a thick V-shaped ribbon.

steps.title: Pipe
steps.text: Fill the piping bag and pipe an 8 cm ring onto each oiled paper square. Set them on the tray and chill for 15 min.

steps.title: Heat the oil
steps.text: Pour oil into the wide pan until it is roughly 4 cm deep (half full at most) and bring it up to 180 °C on the thermometer.

steps.title: Fry
steps.text: Slide 3 crullers into the oil paper side up and lift the paper away with tongs after about 30 seconds. Fry 2-3 min a side at 175-185 °C, until deep golden, puffed and very light, with no pale damp seams in the ridges. Drain on the rack and cool for 10 min.

steps.title: Glaze
steps.text: Whisk the icing sugar, honey, hot water and vanilla into a thin, smooth glaze. Dip each cruller all over, let the excess drip away and leave on the rack for 10 min until the glaze sets glassy.

tips: The most common mistake is pulling them out too soon; underfried crullers collapse as they cool, so fry until the ridges are deep golden.
Do not skip cooking the paste on the heat; drying it is what lets it hold the eggs and puff.
Pipe with a large open star nozzle so the ridges stay deep.
Thin the glaze with a few drops more water if it looks opaque.

Frying safety: use a heavy, deep pot no more than half full of oil, with a clip-on thermometer, and dry the food before it goes in. Never leave hot oil unattended. If the oil catches fire, turn off the heat and cover the pot with a metal lid or use a fire extinguisher; never use water.
Don't taste the raw dough or batter: raw flour and raw egg aren't safe to eat until baked.
storage: Best within a few hours. Keep uncovered at room temperature on the day; they soften in a box.
